Dear Baljeet paaji,
You asked in your last message whether I've started my chemistry project on polymers. Technically, no. But I have a plan. I work way better under pressure, you know that. Remember my Class 9 model? Built the night before, and it got an A. So there's no point starting now when the deadline is ten days away.
Also, I've been watching videos about polymers, which counts as research. Tonight I'll watch just one more and then open the file.
Honestly, when I open the project sheet, it's full of words like "monomer" and "condensation", and my head goes a bit blank. It's easier to close it and do it later, when I'm in the mood.
Anyway, how's college in Patiala? Is the canteen food as bad as you said?
Your cousin,
Lokesh

qa.q: What happened with Lokesh's Class 9 model?
qa.a: It was built the night before, and it got an A.

qa.q: What does Lokesh's head going 'a bit blank' suggest about the real reason for the delay?
qa.a: It suggests the delay is about avoiding the uncomfortable feeling of not understanding words like 'monomer', not about having plenty of time.

qa.q: What could Lokesh try instead of 'one more video' tonight?
qa.a: Lokesh could open the sheet and look up just one confusing word, or ask Baljeet paaji to explain 'monomer', so the blank feeling shrinks.

qa.q: How might Baljeet paaji read this letter?
qa.a: Baljeet may smile at the 'pressure' excuse but notice the line about the blank head and guess that Lokesh feels nervous about the topic.

grounding: Shows a teenager giving reasonable-sounding excuses for delaying a project while the real reason is avoiding the uncomfortable feeling of not understanding it.

Charu, trust me, your friend Rekha has it sorted. The history essay's due Monday, it's Friday, that's like three whole days. I always do better at the last minute anyway; my brain just switches on.
Right now I'm only watching one video, then I'll start. Okay, maybe this one too, it's only twelve minutes. It's basically a break before the real work, which is supposed to be good for you, right?
Why are you looking at me like that?
Fine. The truth is, last time Mrs Dsouza wrote "shallow analysis" in red across the top, and every time I open the document I see those words. So yes, I'd rather watch someone fold paper cranes. At least nobody writes in red on paper cranes.
Okay, don't laugh. You're laughing.
One more video. Then the essay. Probably.

qa.q: What did Mrs Dsouza write across Rekha's last essay?
qa.a: "Shallow analysis", in red across the top.

qa.q: Why would Rekha rather watch videos than open the essay?
qa.a: Every time the document opens, Rekha sees 'shallow analysis' in red, so the videos are a way to avoid that sting of being judged.

qa.q: What could Charu suggest to help Rekha start?
qa.a: Charu could suggest writing just one messy first sentence together, or asking Mrs Dsouza what deeper analysis looks like, so the red words feel less scary.

Saturday, 9:30 pm
This afternoon I was supposed to revise the geometry chapter. I opened the book, looked at the theorems and felt like lying down on the floor. Then Vishal shouted from the next terrace that the wind was perfect for kites. I told myself I'd revise after.
The second I shut the book, I felt SO light. Like taking off a heavy school bag. We flew kites till sunset and I laughed so much.
But since about 7 there's been this small buzzing feeling in my stomach, like when you can't remember if you locked the door. Through dinner, through TV. It's still here.
Funny thing is, last Saturday I did exactly the same with the history chapter, and it felt exactly the same. Light, then buzzing.
Test is Tuesday. I'll do it tomorrow. Probably.
Rajni

qa.a: That the wind was perfect for kites.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel the moment the book shut, and later that evening?
qa.a: Rajni felt light, like taking off a heavy school bag, and then from about 7 a small buzzing guilt that stayed through dinner and TV.

qa.q: What could Rajni try tomorrow so the pattern doesn't repeat?
qa.a: Rajni could do one theorem before any break, so the light feeling comes after starting rather than after avoiding.

qa.q: What might Vishal have noticed about Rajni on the terrace?
qa.a: Vishal probably saw a friend laughing and relaxed, with no idea that a geometry chapter was waiting and guilt would follow.

grounding: Shows the instant lift of putting off revision, the background hum of guilt afterwards, and the pattern repeating because the relief feels rewarding.

passage:
At 9 pm on Wednesday, with the sociology essay due at 9 am, Fatima finally opened a blank document in her Glasgow flat. Two weeks of "later" had turned into this.
Her heart was hammering, and for once the fear worked like fuel. She typed without stopping, three mugs of tea going cold beside her. At 3 am she snapped at Ada for asking, kindly, whether she wanted toast. At 8:52 she hit submit on a conclusion she hadn't reread.
A week later the mark came back: 64, a solid pass. "See?" she told Ada, waving her phone. "I work best under pressure."
She didn't mention the tutor's comment about the "rushed final section", or the two days of headache afterwards, or the apology she still owed Ada for the toast.
Next essay's due in three weeks, she thought. Plenty of time.

qa.q: What mark did Fatima's essay get?
qa.a: 64, a solid pass.

qa.q: What does Fatima's 'See? I work best under pressure' reveal about what she learned?
qa.a: She believes the overnight sprint proves delaying is fine, ignoring the rushed section, the headaches and snapping at Ada.

qa.q: What could Fatima notice before the next essay?
qa.a: She could count the hidden costs, the tutor's comment, two days of headache and the strain with Ada, and start a small piece early instead of relying on panic.

qa.q: How might Ada have felt at 3 am when offering toast?
qa.a: Ada was trying to be kind and got snapped at, so Ada may have felt hurt and may still be waiting for an apology.

grounding: Shows fear finally powering an overnight essay that gets a decent mark, teaching the student that delay works while the costs go unnoticed.

During submission week the computer lab on the second floor of the engineering block stayed open till 6 am, and at 1:40 am Nikita was one of eleven people still there. The data structures assignment had been set a month ago. She had started it at 8 pm.
Now, with hours left, fear finally pushed her fingers faster than they had moved all semester. Tanuja, two seats down, had finished days ago and stayed only to keep her company. "You okay?"
"Never better," Nikita said, eyes red, debugging line 214.
At 5:58 she uploaded it. Two test cases failed; the rest passed. She got 17 out of 20.
On the walk back to the hostel she felt almost triumphant. "Honestly, if I'd started early I'd have overthought it."
Tanuja said nothing about the dosa Nikita had skipped, the 9 am lab she was about to sleep through, or her shaking hands.

qa.q: What score did Nikita get on the assignment?
qa.a: She got 17 out of 20.

qa.q: Why did Nikita feel almost triumphant on the walk back?
qa.a: The overnight sprint worked well enough that she took it as proof that starting early would only have made her overthink.

qa.q: What went wrong beneath the good score, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Two test cases failed, she skipped food, her hands shook and she was about to miss a 9 am lab; starting a small piece in the first week could spare those costs.

qa.q: What might Tanuja be thinking as they walk back?
qa.a: Tanuja, who stayed only for company, may notice the skipped meal and shaking hands and feel worried, but chooses silence over a lecture at dawn.

grounding: Illustrates a last-minute overnight sprint in a college lab that earns a good score and reinforces delay, while the stress and quality costs are brushed aside.

The hostel room Farida shared with Nandini was so small that their beds touched, and on Tuesday night Nandini's phone call home filled every corner of it. Farida lay facing the wall.
She had submitted her marketing report at 11:58 that morning, two minutes before the portal closed, after another all-nighter. "You are so lazy," she told herself silently. "Useless. Every single time."
She made the vow again, the fourth this semester: from tomorrow, a new timetable, up at six, no phone.
On Wednesday the next assignment came out. Farida opened the brief, and the moment she saw it the voice started again: you'll just mess this one up too. Her chest went tight. She closed the laptop and picked up her phone.
"I'll start after lunch," she told Nandini, who had finally hung up.
By Friday she still hadn't opened it again.

qa.q: What time did Farida submit her marketing report?
qa.a: At 11:58 that morning, two minutes before the portal closed.

qa.q: Why did Farida's chest go tight when she opened the new brief?
qa.a: The harsh voice calling her lazy and predicting she would mess up again made the new task feel threatening before she even began.

qa.q: What could break Farida's loop instead of another vow?
qa.a: Speaking to herself more kindly after a late submission and taking one small step on the new brief, rather than a whole new timetable, would ease the discomfort that keeps her avoiding.

qa.q: What might Nandini notice about Farida this week?
qa.a: Nandini may only see Farida on her phone saying she'll start after lunch, unaware of the harsh voice and the tight chest behind it.

grounding: Shows a student calling herself lazy after a last-minute submission, vowing to change, then avoiding the next task because the harsh self-talk makes it feel worse.

On the wall above Jatin's desk in the Malviya Nagar flat hung three sheets of paper, each titled NEW ME in thick marker: January, March, and one he had written at 2 am last night after missing the college design competition by a day.
"Nikamma," he muttered at his reflection in the dark laptop screen. "Good-for-nothing. Always the same."
His cousin Ramesh, who shared the flat, came in with two cups of chai. "Another NEW ME?"
"This time I mean it. No more delays."
By Saturday the next task was due: a logo for their uncle's shop. Every time Jatin sat down, the word nikamma sounded in his head, and designing felt heavier than ever. He cleaned the kitchen instead. Twice.
Ramesh watched him scrub the same pan and said quietly, "You're not lazy, yaar. You're scared of that word you keep calling yourself."

qa.q: What title was written on each of the three sheets above Jatin's desk?
qa.a: NEW ME, in thick marker.

qa.q: Why did designing the logo feel heavier than ever to Jatin?
qa.a: Each time he sat down, the word 'nikamma' sounded in his head, so the task carried the sting of his own harsh judgement.

qa.q: What turning point does Ramesh's remark open?
qa.a: It invites Jatin to see that harsh self-talk, not laziness, is making tasks harder, so he could drop the insults and start the logo with one small step.

qa.q: What might Ramesh be feeling as he watches Jatin scrub the same pan?
qa.a: Ramesh seems worried and caring, recognising the pattern of vows and avoidance and wanting Jatin to stop calling himself names.

grounding: Illustrates a young man's cycle of calling himself useless, writing new vows and then avoiding the next task as the self-criticism makes it heavier.

Trisha, you've been staring at that blank page since lunch. Your Deepika Masi has been there.
In my final year in Pune, I had a dissertation on river pollution that I couldn't start for a month. Every time I sat down I wanted it to open like a published paper. So I wrote nothing.
Then my hostel friend Leena dragged me to the university library at 7 am and set her little kitchen timer for twenty-five minutes. "Write the worst first paragraph you can," she said. "Bad on purpose."
I wrote something terrible about rivers being "very important and also wet". We both laughed. But then the second sentence came, and the third, and by the time the timer rang I didn't want to stop. We went back every morning for three weeks.
So, beta, pack your bag. Library, timer, one ugly paragraph. I'll drive you.

qa.a: Twenty-five minutes.

With her cousin's wedding three days away, Sangeeta's house in Mylapore was full of relatives, a nadaswaram rehearsal and the endless clatter of steel vessels. Her psychology term paper was due Monday, and she hadn't written a word. Every time she sat on the bed with her laptop, an aunt needed help with garlands.
On Thursday Gopika texted: "Library. 4 pm. Bring only your laptop."
The small branch library near the temple tank closed at six, which gave them under two hours. Gopika set a phone timer for fifteen minutes. "Rule: you write rubbish. One paragraph. No deleting."
Sangeeta wrote a clumsy paragraph about memory and exam stress, with one sentence that didn't even end. When the timer rang she was halfway into the second paragraph and waved Gopika off.
By six she had two pages, messy but real. On the walk home through the wedding noise, the paper didn't frighten her anymore.

qa.q: What time did the branch library close?
qa.a: It closed at six.

qa.q: How had Sangeeta's feelings about the paper changed by the walk home?
qa.a: The paper no longer frightened her, because she now had two real pages, however messy 😊.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Gopika's rule of a fifteen-minute timer and one rubbish paragraph with no deleting lowered the bar, so starting felt safe and momentum carried Sangeeta further.

qa.a: Gopika likely felt pleased and a little amused, seeing that the small start had turned into real momentum.

Monday, week one. Jagdish, who managed the content team at a small Pune publisher, noticed that Preeti had missed another soft deadline, the third this month. Her chapter summaries came in late on Friday nights, and they were the best on the team. He caught himself drafting a message: "Please be more disciplined." He deleted it.
Wednesday, week two. He asked her to walk with him to the chai stall. "Your work is excellent. The late part puzzles me. What makes these tasks hard to start?"
Preeti was quiet a long moment. "Honestly? I'm never sure what length you want. And after the sales team called my first draft 'amateur' in March, I rewrite everything five times before anyone sees it."
Friday, week three. Jagdish now sent a one-line scope with every brief and a mid-week note: "Send me a rough draft. Rough is fine."
Preeti's summary arrived on Thursday afternoon.

qa.q: How many soft deadlines had Preeti missed that month by week one?
qa.a: She had missed the third soft deadline this month.

qa.q: What fear or worry was really making Preeti delay?
qa.a: She was unsure what length was wanted and still afraid of being called 'amateur', so she rewrote everything five times before showing anyone.

qa.q: Which changes did Jagdish make, and why did they work?
qa.a: He added a one-line scope and a mid-week request for a rough draft, which cleared the unclear scope and eased her fear of judgement.

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt when Jagdish asked what made the tasks hard?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved and respected, since he asked instead of judging her character, which made it safe to admit the fear.

grounding: Shows a manager who notices a capable employee's late but strong work and, by asking what makes tasks hard, uncovers unclear scope and fear.

Nikita, you said your new analyst keeps sending things at the last minute, and you're ready to write "lacks discipline" in his review. Your Gautam uncle made that exact mistake once.
The first team I led, at twenty-six, was in a bank in Kochi. There was a young man, Suresh, bright as anything. Every report late, every report excellent. I decided he was careless, and one day I said so in front of the team. He went red and said nothing. Things got worse.
Months later, over lunch, I finally asked, "What makes these reports hard for you?" It all came out. He was doing his own work and covering for a colleague on leave, and nobody had told him which reports came first. He was drowning and too proud to say it. I felt terrible.
So before you write that review, Nikita, ask him one question. Not "Why are you late?" but "What makes this hard?"

qa.q: Where did Gautam lead a team at twenty-six?
qa.a: In a bank in Kochi.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel after learning why Suresh was late?
qa.a: He felt terrible, realising Suresh had been drowning in work and unclear priorities, not being careless.

qa.q: What does Gautam advise Nikita to do before writing the review?
qa.a: Ask the analyst 'What makes this hard?' instead of judging his discipline, since the answer may reveal overload, unclear scope or fear.

qa.q: What might Suresh have felt when Gautam called him careless in front of the team?
qa.a: Suresh likely felt humiliated and unseen, already overloaded and too proud to explain, which is why he went red and said nothing.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a manager who judged a late but capable employee's character before asking and finding overload and unclear priorities.

Tuesday night
Third day avoiding the grant proposal. Tonight, instead of calling myself lazy, I tried Reena's trick from the workshop: write down exactly what feels bad about the task.
So here goes.
1. The budget section. I genuinely don't know how to do it. Unclear steps, not laziness.
2. Dr Mathew will read it. After he tore apart my last draft in the meeting, I feel sick imagining his face. That's fear of being judged.
3. The background section. Honestly just boring. I've written it three times for other proposals.
Looking at the list, it isn't one big monster. It's three small, different problems.
Fixes: email the finance office tomorrow for the budget template. Ask Reena if she'll read my draft before Dr Mathew does. Reuse and update the old background and stop pretending it has to be art.
Already feel lighter.
Joseph

qa.q: Whose trick did Joseph try tonight?
qa.a: Reena's trick from the workshop.

qa.q: What feeling did Joseph find behind avoiding the part Dr Mathew will read?
qa.a: Fear of being judged; Joseph feels sick imagining Dr Mathew's face after the last draft was torn apart in a meeting.

qa.q: How does naming each feeling point Joseph to a fix?
qa.a: Unclear steps lead to asking the finance office for a template, fear of judgement to asking Reena for an early read, and boredom to reusing the old background.

qa.a: Reena may be glad the workshop trick helped and happy to give a kinder first read, knowing it eases Joseph's fear.

Nitin worked the night shift at a call centre in Noida and slept through the loud afternoons of his family's two-room flat, so the bank exam books had sat untouched for weeks. Every time he looked at them, he heard all the months he'd wasted.
On Sunday night, before leaving for work, he did something small. He cleared one corner of the kitchen table and set out the reasoning book open at chapter one, a pencil, his earplugs and a sticky note: "Five minutes. That's all."
Then he said out loud to the empty kitchen, "Okay. The last months are done. I'm not going to punish myself for them."
His sister Hafsa, filling her water bottle, raised an eyebrow. "Talking to the table now?"
At 3 pm on Monday, groggy, he sat down because everything was already there. Five minutes turned into forty. When he stopped, he didn't feel guilty about the lost months. He felt like someone who had started.

qa.q: What did Nitin's sticky note say?
qa.a: "Five minutes. That's all."

qa.q: Why did Nitin say he wouldn't punish himself for the last months?
qa.a: He knew the guilt about wasted months made the books feel heavy, so forgiving himself would make them easier to face.

qa.q: Which small steps made Monday's start easy?
qa.a: Setting up the table the night before with the book open, a pencil and earplugs, and promising only five minutes, so there was nothing to decide in the groggy afternoon.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see her brother talking to the table?
qa.a: Hafsa teases him about it, but she may soon notice that her brother has quietly started studying after weeks.

grounding: Shows a young man with little quiet time committing to five minutes, setting up his workspace the night before and forgiving past delays.

In Class 9B, Rehana Ma'am held up Jyoti's biology notebook for everyone to see: diagrams labelled in two colours, not a single cut, the margins ruled in pencil. "This is how a notebook should look," she said. Jyoti's cheeks went warm.
At home, Amma had pinned her report card to the fridge for the third year running, and Appa told every visitor, "Our Jyoti never makes mistakes." Jyoti liked being that girl. It felt like armour. People asked to borrow her notes.
That evening, copying the digestive system, she smudged one label. She tore out the whole page and started again, then again, until it was perfect at 11 pm.
As she switched off the lamp, a small thought slid in: what would they say if one day it wasn't perfect? She pushed it away and fell asleep.

qa.a: In pencil.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti tear out a whole page over one smudged label?

qa.a: They could praise her effort, curiosity or a brave mistake, so Jyoti learns she is valued even when a page isn't perfect.

qa.a: They likely see her as effortlessly perfect, without knowing about the torn pages and the late night behind them.

In third-period literature at his school in Seville, Mateo's eraser was down to a grey stub. He had written the first line of his analysis four times and rubbed it out four times, and the paper was going thin.
When Señora Ruiz asked who could explain the poem's final image, Mateo knew the answer, or thought he did. He kept his hand flat on the desk. Fatima, beside him, answered instead, half right, and just laughed when the teacher corrected her. Mateo couldn't understand how she could laugh.

The chemistry lab at Arohi's school smelled of spirit lamps, and her practical file was the neatest in the batch. Today's titration, though, would not behave. Her first reading was 21.4. It should have matched her second, 21.1. She covered it with correction fluid, then again, until the paper went bumpy.
Kamal, her lab partner, said, "Just write both. Sir said slight differences are normal." Arohi shook her head.
When the teacher asked the class for their final value, she knew roughly what hers was but kept her eyes on the burette. Kamal answered for both of them.
At the end of the period she noticed a tiny spill of solution on her file cover, and her throat closed. She scrubbed at it with a tissue, nearly in tears, while Kamal stared. "Arohi, it's a file. It's fine."
It didn't feel fine. It felt as if everything she was had a stain on it.

qa.q: What were Arohi's two titration readings?
Why did the small spill on her file cover make Arohi's throat close?
qa.a: For her any flaw feels like a stain on her whole worth, so even a small spill felt unbearable.

qa.q: How could the chemistry teacher help Arohi at this stage?
qa.a: The teacher could show that recording real readings, even mismatched ones, is good science, praise honest work over neatness, and gently check in about how upset she gets.

qa.q: What might Kamal be feeling watching Arohi scrub the file?
qa.a: Kamal seems surprised and worried, unable to understand why something so small upsets her, and tries to reassure her.

grounding: Illustrates a student who rewrites readings, avoids answering unless sure and is near tears over a small spill, as each task threatens her sense of worth.
